cards.front: Ordinary income (for tax purposes)
cards.back: The combination of earned income, investment (portfolio) income, and passive income. Ordinary income determines the investor's income tax rate. Short-term capital gains are also taxed at ordinary income rates.

cards.front: Earned income
cards.back: Income derived from active participation in a trade or business — salary, wages, bonuses, tips, and consulting fees. Eligibility for IRA contributions is based only on earned income.

cards.front: Investment (portfolio) income
cards.back: Income earned from investments held by the investor, including dividends and interest payments. Short-term capital gains are added to ordinary income for tax purposes.

cards.front: Passive income
cards.back: Investment income derived from direct participation programs (DPPs) such as limited partnerships and many real estate investments. Passive losses may only offset passive income — not earned or portfolio income.

cards.front: What is the only type of income that passive losses may be used to offset?
cards.back: Passive income only. Passive losses cannot offset earned income or portfolio (investment) income.

cards.front: How is the holding period distinguished between short-term and long-term capital gains?
cards.back: Short-term: held for one year or less — taxed as ordinary income. Long-term: held for more than one year — taxed at preferential long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

cards.front: How are long-term capital gains taxed compared to short-term capital gains?
cards.back: Long-term capital gains are taxed at preferential rates (0%, 15%, or 20%) that are generally lower than ordinary income rates. Short-term capital gains are taxed at ordinary income rates.

cards.front: What is the Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) and when does it apply?
cards.back: An additional 3.8% tax applied to net investment income (including capital gains, dividends, and interest) for taxpayers with modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) above specified thresholds.

cards.front: How may capital losses be used against capital gains and ordinary income?
cards.back: Capital losses offset capital gains dollar-for-dollar. Net losses exceeding gains may offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year. Any remaining losses carry forward indefinitely until used.

cards.front: An investor has $24,000 in capital gains and $32,000 in capital losses this year. How are these treated for tax purposes?
cards.back: Net loss = $8,000. Up to $3,000 may offset ordinary income this year. The remaining $5,000 carries forward to the next tax year (indefinitely until used).

cards.front: A customer has $120,000 in ordinary income, a $47,000 capital gain, and a $50,000 capital loss for the year. How much taxable income will the customer report?
cards.back: The $47,000 gain is fully offset by $50,000 in losses. The remaining $3,000 of losses reduces ordinary income: $120,000 − $3,000 = $117,000 ordinary income, zero net gains.

cards.front: A client buys stock on July 10 for $18 and sells it on June 10 of the following year for $22. What is the tax treatment?
cards.back: Holding period is 11 months — one year or less — so this is a short-term capital gain of $4 per share, taxed as ordinary income.

cards.front: What is the tax impact of an unrealized gain or loss?
cards.back: None. Unrealized gains/losses exist on open positions and have no tax consequences. Taxes are due only when the position is closed and the gain or loss is realized.

cards.front: Wash sale rule
cards.back: If an investor sells a security at a loss and purchases the same or substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed. The disallowed loss is added to the cost basis of the replacement security.

cards.front: What is the wash sale window?
cards.back: 30 days before AND 30 days after the date of the sale that created the loss (a 61-day window total). Repurchasing the same or substantially identical security within this period disallows the loss.

cards.front: What securities are considered 'substantially identical' for wash sale purposes?
cards.back: Any security that can be converted or exercised into the security sold for a loss — including call options, rights, warrants, and convertible bonds or convertible preferred stock from the same issuer.

cards.front: On November 17, an investor sells 1,000 XYZ at $28 (originally bought at $30 — establishing a $2,000 loss). On November 23, the investor buys 1,000 XYZ at $27. What is the tax treatment?
cards.back: Wash sale — the repurchase occurred within 30 days of the loss sale. The $2,000 loss is disallowed for current tax purposes and is added to the cost basis of the newly purchased shares.

cards.front: Is a wash sale itself illegal?
cards.back: No. The wash sale transaction is not illegal. What is prohibited is claiming the disallowed loss as a tax deduction.

cards.front: What holding period is required for a dividend to be 'qualified' and taxed at the long-term capital gains rate?
cards.back: The investor must hold the underlying common stock for more than 60 days during the 121-day period beginning 60 days before the ex-dividend date.

cards.front: Which of the following is NOT taxed as ordinary income: a bonus, bond interest, profit from sale of a long-held security, or consulting fees?
cards.back: Profit from the sale of a long-held (more than one year) security — that is a long-term capital gain, taxed at preferential rates. Bonuses and consulting fees are earned income; bond interest is portfolio income — all taxed as ordinary income.
